Sample text:
---
Okay, you asked for it — here's what's been rattling around in my head lately:

### The Night Shift at the Department of Misplaced Dreams

I work the night shift on the third floor of a building that isn't on any map. It's wedged between a dentist's office and a shop that only sells keys. The sign on our door just says LOST. People almost never find us on purpose.

They send in reports. Or they dream about coming to report, which is how most of them arrive. A form appears on the desk, filled out in handwriting that gets shakier the longer the dream has been missing.

*What did it feel like?*
*What color was it?*
*Did it have teeth?*

We file them in tall, wooden cabinets that sigh when you open them. The top drawer is very thin and light — dreams about falling, dreams about flying but badly. The middle drawer is heavier — dreams about being late, about showing up to an exam naked, about forgetting your own name at a party. 

The bottom drawer we don't open after noon. That's dreams about teeth.

Some dreams arrive leaking. A dream about rain will soak the whole cabinet if you don't dry it out properly. A dream about your childhood house will smell faintly of cut grass for three weeks. A dream about an argument you never had will give everyone on the floor a headache.

My job isn't really to return them. My job is to keep them from wandering too far into other people's sleep.

Once, a woman reported a dream she'd lost in 1987. She described it in perfect detail: a green bicycle, a long hill, a man at the top waving at her even though she didn't know him. I checked the ledger under G. For Green. There it was, folded up small as a handkerchief.

When I played it back for her, she went very quiet. 

"I didn't remember the bell," she said. "It had a bell."

She didn't ask for it back. She just said, "I can let it go now." And the dream, relieved, went off on its own. That's the best part of the job, I've found. Not finding. Letting go.

On Tuesdays the new ones wash in. I find them in coat pockets and library books and under radiators that no one has used since summer. Last Tuesday I found a goldfish that could fly, still damp. A little boy must have lost it. It kept trying to turn in mid-air, like it was swimming.

I put it in a jar of water on my desk for the night, just in case he calls. He hasn't yet, but it's happy enough. It eats the air.

In the early morning I clock out, buy bread from the bakery that sells out by seven, and walk home through an ordinary street where everyone is just waking up and blinking. Nobody there knows what they dreamed. Nobody needs to.

And for a little while, walking home, I don't think about it at all.
---

The voice is calm and quietly attentive, treating dreams as delicate things with textures, smells, and moods of their own. Its pathos comes from the small moment when a woman recognizes a detail in a long-lost dream and is able to release it. The closing walk home offers the reader a soft landing: the speaker can leave this strange work behind for a while, even as its tenderness lingers.

## What the model chose to foreground
The piece foregrounds lost dreams, ordinary objects made uncanny—cabinets, coat pockets, a jar—and the distinction between recovering something and letting it go. Its chosen mood is more wistful than eerie: even the strange dreams are handled with care, and the goldfish is allowed to be happy in its improvised home.

Medium: The coherent imagery and recurring emphasis on gentle care and release make this a distinctive expressive choice, especially in its quiet resolution.
